analysis.one_liner: Requires warrants for searches of Americans' communications collected under foreign surveillance law and bans buying broker data.
analysis.headline: Five cosponsors joined the Republican sponsor, but the bill has seen no hearing, markup, or vote since its March 2026 referral to two House committees.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put court-approved warrants in front of government searches of Americans' phone and internet communications collected under the foreign surveillance law known as Section 702, require warrants for location tracking, web browsing and search history, and ban federal law enforcement from buying Americans' personal data from commercial data brokers. It also imposes retention limits so data on Americans is destroyed within five years, restricts the use of surveillance-derived information in court, and adds outside privacy experts to the secret surveillance court. In exchange, it reauthorizes the underlying Section 702 program for four more years, through April 2030.
analysis.who_benefits: Every American whose calls, texts, emails, location, browsing history, or connected-car data could be swept into foreign-intelligence collection — including people who are only one hop away from a foreign target. The warrant requirement means the government can no longer search that material for an American's communications without going to a judge, except in emergencies with after-the-fact reporting.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Americans' calls, texts, and location data

how_it_helps.text: Bar federal agencies from searching communications collected under Section 702 for information about Americans or anyone inside the U.S. without a court order or warrant, with narrow exceptions for emergencies, consent, and defensive cybersecurity — each of which must be reported to the court and Congress within 14 days.

Ban federal law enforcement from buying Americans' personal data — including biometric and location information — from commercial data brokers, closing the workaround of purchasing data the government could not legally compel.

Prohibit 'reverse targeting' — aiming foreign surveillance at a non-American primarily to collect on a known person inside the United States — and limit the use of Section 702-derived information in criminal, civil, and administrative proceedings.
Require that information about covered persons be destroyed within five years of collection unless it is tied to specific litigation or an authorized investigation.
Require warrants for government access to location information, web browsing records, and search query records, extend email privacy protections, and bar warrantless federal searches of car data.

Require court approval before the government can force technical assistance from communications providers, expand privacy and technical experts ('amici') in the secret Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, and allow those experts to seek review of court decisions all the way to the Supreme Court.

analysis.who_pays: Federal intelligence and law enforcement agencies give up their current ability to search collected communications for Americans' data without a warrant and to buy commercial data directly, and must document every query they run. Data brokers lose a major class of government customers. Communications providers gain some protection from sweeping assistance demands but face new documentation and court-approval requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Spy agencies, federal police, and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The bill reauthorizes Section 702 for four more years, through April 20, 2030, so opponents of the underlying program see it as locking in a collection authority they want ended.

The data-broker ban contains carve-outs: agencies can still obtain 'lawfully obtained public data' with attestations, and the prohibition does not apply to whistleblower bounty programs, background checks with consent, or certain large data compilations the agency cannot reasonably filter.

Emergency and cybersecurity exceptions let officials access covered information first and report to the court and Congress within 14 days afterward, and much of the enforcement relies on the agencies' own compliance records and annual reports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy gains are concrete and wide-reaching: a warrant before the government searches your communications, a ban on buying your data from brokers, and limits on retention and courtroom use. The main concessions — a four-year extension of the 702 program and a set of emergency, cybersecurity, and public-data exceptions — are real, but the bill's compliance mechanics depend heavily on agencies policing themselves and reporting violations, so its strength would depend on the oversight it creates actually being used.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2026 and sent to the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees, and since then nothing further has happened — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Warren Davidson (R-OH) introduced the Government Surveillance Reform Act of 2026 on March 12, 2026, joined on introduction by Reps. Zoe Lofgren, Pramila Jayapal, and Sara Jacobs.
The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, with the timing of consideration left to the Speaker.
No further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — is recorded in the bill's action history.
The bill has five cosponsors in addition to the sponsor: four Democrats and one Republican.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As long as the bill sits without action, federal intelligence and law-enforcement agencies keep their current warrantless query authorities, and data brokers keep a large government customer base. No one's privacy protections have changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Spy agencies and data brokers, for now

against.role: Agencies that operate Section 702 and related collection authorities
against.what_they_did: Have repeatedly and publicly opposed warrant requirements for searching Americans' communications collected under Section 702 in past reauthorization fights, the same central restriction this bill would impose.

sides.party_line_note: The bill pairs a Republican sponsor with four Democratic cosponsors and one more Republican — a civil-liberties coalition that crosses party lines rather than a party split; no roll calls have occurred.

industries.industry: Federal intelligence and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies would lose warrantless access to Americans' communications and the ability to buy commercial personal data, but would gain four more years of certainty for the Section 702 program. Their preference in past fights has been reauthorization without the warrant conditions, which is what the bill adds.

Federal law enforcement would be barred from buying Americans' personal data, including biometric and location information, ending a market in which brokers sell data the government could not legally compel. State and local agencies using federal funds would have to publicly report any such purchases.

industries.industry: Telecom, cloud, and internet communications providers
industries.note: Providers would gain court oversight of government technical-assistance demands and relief from directives under the expanded 'electronic communication service provider' definition, with some past directives declared void. They would face new documentation and court-order requirements in exchange.

analysis.trajectory: Section 702 was already extended through April 2030 by earlier law, so there is no expiration deadline to force action, and surveillance bills sent to the Intelligence Committee rarely reach the floor without a scheduled markup. With no committee action in the months since referral and only five cosponsors, the most likely path is that the bill sits until this Congress ends — unless a reauthorization-adjacent fight or a surveillance scandal creates pressure to move it.
